newsitem.title: USA: Gulfstream gets mixed reviews, faces competition. [CORRECTED]
newsitem.headline: Gulfstream gets mixed reviews, faces competition. [CORRECTED]

text.p: Gulfstream Aerospace Corp 's $644 million initial public offering should be well received, but aerospace analysts warn the corporate jet maker will face tough competition for its new long-range G-V aircraft within a year.

Gulfstream's "going to have an excellent 1997. But you have to look beyond the first year to properly value the stock," Robert Natale, director of equity research at Standard & Poors, who tracks new stock offerings said.

Gulfstream's new G-V aircraft has a one-year lead on the competition, but its potential market will shrink starting in 1997 as Boeing Co and Canada's Bombardier Inc launch comparable products, some aerospace analysts said.
Gulfstream has an order backlog of about 64 G-V jets, the first of which will be delivered by year-end.
Randall Greene, an aerospace consultant with Aeronautical Systems in Colorado doubts Gulfstream can meet analysts' projections for sales of up to 350 to 500 G-V planes over the next decade.

"There's no way Gulfstream can have the projected sales they say," Greene said. "Gulfstream's pretty much dominated the high-end of the corporate jet business for 30 years or so, but that's without much competition."
Most of Gulfstream's jets are sold to repeat customers. But the G-V offers "only 25 percent more performance, but a 50 percent increase in price" than the previous G-IV model, Greene said.
At the hefty price tag of over $30 million, the "potential market is already smaller than for Gulfstream's earlier products. But with competition, the market really shrinks," Greene said.
Gulfstream's 19-passenger G-V is also virtually identical in payload, speed and price as Bombardier's jet, analysts said. The competing aircrafts also have the same engine.
Greene expects Gulfstream to sell about 150 G-V planes over the next decade, compared to total sales of about 270 G-IV planes, Gulfstream's earlier model.
Wolfgang Demisch, an aerospace analyst with BT Securities, is more bullish, saying Gulfstream will benefit from the increased globalization of business and growing Asian demand.
"The market for long-range planes with trans-Pacific capabilities will be surprisingly good," giving both Gulfstream and Bombardier "room to co-exist," Demisch said.
Demisch said he expects sales of G-V caliber products to reach up to 1,000 jets over 20 years.

Regardless of the long-range sales forecasts, some analysts who track new stock offerings say Gulfstream's initial stock offering will be well received by institutional investors attracted by its worldwide name recognition.
John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket, says Gulfstream's 28 million share offering in early October "should be hot."
"But that depends what you're in there for," Fitzgibbon said. If you're in this for a flip, it's not bad."
"We're pretty neutral on the deal," said Steven Tuen, an analyst with IPO Value Monitor.

Gulfstream recently narrowed the expected price range for the offering to $22 to $24 a share, from an original range of $21 to $25 a share, according to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
Other analysts said they are concerned about Gulfstream's 18 percent (corrects from 230 percent) debt-to-capital ratio.
"We have an 'avoid' on this stock. But there are probably enough believers out there that they will able to pull this (offering) off," Standard & Poor's Natale said.
Proceeds from the offering will go to Fortsmann Little & Co and other selling shareholders, not back into Gulfstream - which also has become a concern for some investors.
Forstmann acquire Gulfstream in 1990 through a leveraged buyout. The corporate jet maker's first attempt at a public offering failed in 1992.
